summary: This document specifies the Diameter SIP application, in which a Diameter client co-located with a SIP server can ask a Diameter server to authenticate users and authorize use of SIP resources.

plainLanguage.summary: A phone-call server can ask a central office whether a caller is who they say and may use the service. This describes how it asks.

questions: what is the diameter sip application
what are diameter uar and mar commands
how does diameter authenticate sip users
what is the diameter subscriber locator
subtitle: How a SIP server asks a Diameter server who a user is, what they may do, and where to route them.

tldr.problem: A SIP server needs to authenticate users and authorize their use of SIP services, and it needs user profiles and routing hints, but the user data lives in a central database outside the SIP server.
tldr.mechanism: The SIP server embeds a Diameter client and exchanges six request/answer pairs with a Diameter server: UAR/UAA, SAR/SAA, LIR/LIA, MAR/MAA, RTR/RTA and PPR/PPA. HTTP Digest credentials are checked either in the Diameter server or, optionally, in the SIP server.
tldr.outcome: RFC 4740 is a Proposed Standard that defines the Diameter SIP application, with Application-ID 6 and command codes 283 to 288. It has not been obsoleted or updated.

today: RFC 4740 is a Proposed Standard published in November 2006. The metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It builds on the Diameter base protocol in RFC 3588.

sections.title: Why SIP Needs Diameter
sections.content:
RFC 4740 defines the Diameter SIP application. It lets a Diameter client ask a Diameter server for authentication and authorization information about users of SIP-based multimedia services (see RFC 3261 for SIP).

The RFC assumes the SIP server (a proxy, registrar, redirect server or similar) and the Diameter client sit in the same node. The SIP server relies on the Authentication, Authorization, and Accounting (AAA) infrastructure to authenticate SIP requests and to authorize particular SIP services.

The application goes beyond a plain yes or no. It can also download or push updated user profiles, and it offers rudimentary routing help so a SIP server can find the other SIP server assigned to a user. It does not mandate any particular mapping from SIP procedures to Diameter procedures, and the examples in the RFC are informative.
sections.plainLanguage: The phone server asks a central office to check who is calling and what they are allowed to do. The office can also tell it which other phone server looks after that person.

sections.title: Architecture and Assumptions
sections.content:
The RFC assumes a Home Realm made of one or more nodes with Diameter or SIP functions. The user database is outside the SIP node that needs authorization. Data for different users may live on different nodes, but all the data for one user is stored in a single node. That node can be a redundant cluster that looks like one database from outside.

In the main architecture, SIP server 1 sits at the edge of the network and mainly locates SIP server 2. SIP server 2 requests and receives the authentication and authorization data. Both implement a Diameter client. SIP server 1 can be a farm of servers reached through DNS records and needs no Diameter-related state.

When there are many users, a Diameter Subscriber Locator (SL) maps a SIP address-of-record (AOR) to the URI of the Diameter server that holds that user's data. It acts like a Diameter redirect agent: it answers with DIAMETER_REDIRECT_INDICATION and a Redirect-Host AVP, and the client then repeats its request to that server. Several SLs may exist, but they must give equal answers to equal requests.
sections.plainLanguage: Each person's file is kept in exactly one filing cabinet. If the phone server does not know which cabinet, it asks a directory desk, and the desk points to the right one.

sections.title: Typical Call Flows
sections.content:
Section 6 walks through example flows. In the first, a SIP REGISTER reaches SIP server 1. Its Diameter client sends a UAR (User-Authorization-Request) to check that the user may register, and the UAA answer names SIP server 2 or the capabilities needed to pick one. SIP server 2 then sends a MAR (Multimedia-Auth-Request). The Diameter server generates a nonce and replies with a MAA carrying DIAMETER_MULTI_ROUND_AUTH and a challenge, which becomes the SIP 401 response.

When the user retries with credentials, the same UAR/UAA and MAR exchange happens again. The MAA now carries DIAMETER_SUCCESS, the SIP server sends 200 (OK), and it may send a SAR (Server-Assignment-Request) to download the user profile or store its own address. The SAA reply carries zero or more SIP-User-Data AVPs.

Other flows: a stateless outbound proxy can use MAR/MAA alone to challenge with a SIP 407. An edge proxy can use LIR/LIA (Location-Info) to find the SIP server of a request's recipient; any SIP request other than REGISTER triggers an LIR. The Diameter server can push a changed profile with PPR/PPA (Push-Profile).
sections.plainLanguage: Someone knocks and the first guard asks the office if they may enter. A second guard asks the office for a secret question, the visitor answers, and the office says yes. After that the guard can ask for the visitor's details.

sections.title: Commands and Result Codes
sections.content:
Every implementation MUST support twelve commands in six request/answer pairs. Each pair shares a command code: 283 for UAR/UAA, 284 for SAR/SAA, 285 for LIR/LIA, 286 for MAR/MAA, 287 for RTR/RTA and 288 for PPR/PPA. The message formats follow Section 3.2 of RFC 3588.

The UAR carries the SIP-AOR to register, an optional User-Name, and optionally the SIP-Visited-Network-Id and a SIP-User-Authorization-Type. In the answer the Diameter server MUST check that the user exists and that the user may register that AOR. It reports problems with new result codes such as DIAMETER_ERROR_USER_UNKNOWN (5032), DIAMETER_ERROR_IDENTITIES_DONT_MATCH (5033) and, for roaming, DIAMETER_ERROR_ROAMING_NOT_ALLOWED. If a User-Name is needed but missing, it returns DIAMETER_USER_NAME_REQUIRED (4013).

The RFC also defines success codes 2003 to 2008, such as DIAMETER_FIRST_REGISTRATION (2003) and DIAMETER_SUBSEQUENT_REGISTRATION (2004). The SAR's SIP-Server-Assignment-Type AVP has twelve values from NO_ASSIGNMENT (0) to DEREGISTRATION_TOO_MUCH_DATA (11), and says whether the SIP server is reporting a first registration, a refresh, a timeout, a user or administrative deregistration, or an authentication failure.
sections.plainLanguage: There are six kinds of question and answer, like a small set of forms. Each form has a number so everyone knows which one is being used, and the answers use codes for 'yes', 'try again' or 'no'.

sections.title: Authentication Details
sections.content:
The application supports HTTP Digest authentication (RFC 2617), the mechanism SIP mandates. Work derived from Digest, such as Digest using AKA (RFC 3310), also counts as the Digest scheme. Other mechanisms are not currently supported. Digest values travel in Digest-* AVPs inside the grouped SIP-Auth-Data-Item AVP, and nonces are always generated in the Diameter server.

The final check can happen in either place. If the Diameter server wants to authenticate itself, it MUST NOT include a Digest-HA1 AVP in the MAA. If it includes a pre-calculated Digest-HA1 (the H(A1) value), it delegates the final check to the SIP server, saving a round trip. That delegation does not work with the MD5-sess algorithm, because the client nonce may not be known yet.

A SIP request may carry several credentials, for example for different realms. The Diameter client MUST send zero or exactly one credential, chosen by the realm directive, and the realm MUST match the client's own.
sections.plainLanguage: The visitor answers a secret question. Either the office checks the answer, or, to save time, it hands the guard the answer key and the guard checks it.

sections.title: Ending Registrations and Sessions
sections.content:
SIP creates soft state, such as registrations and event subscriptions, that is refreshed or expires. The Diameter server decides whether to map that state onto Diameter user sessions. Implementations MUST support both ways of managing it.

When Diameter sessions are not kept (Auth-Session-State is NO_STATE_MAINTAINED), the client ends the state with a SAR carrying a deregistration type, and the server ends it with a Registration-Termination-Request (RTR). When sessions are kept (STATE_MAINTAINED), the client sends a Session-Termination-Request and the server sends an Abort-Session-Request, as in RFC 3588.
sections.plainLanguage: When a guest leaves, either the guard tells the office, or the office tells the guard to cross the guest off the list. Which note is used depends on how the office keeps its records.

sections.title: Migration from RADIUS
sections.content:
Many Digest AVPs are imported from the RADIUS attribute namespace, which eases migration from the RADIUS Extension for Digest Authentication (RFC 4590). The RFC describes two gateways. From a RADIUS client to a Diameter server, an Access-Request with Digest attributes becomes a MAR, and a DIAMETER_MULTI_ROUND_AUTH answer becomes an Access-Challenge. From a Diameter client to a RADIUS server, the mapping runs the other way.

The match is not complete. The RADIUS extension covers only Digest authentication and has nothing equivalent to UAR/UAA, SAR/SAA, LIR/LIA, RTR/RTA or PPR/PPA.
sections.plainLanguage: An older office used a different form. A translator desk can turn old forms into new ones, but the old form lacks many of the new questions.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
This is an application of Diameter, so the security considerations of RFC 3588 (its Section 13) apply. The Digest discussion in Section 4 of RFC 2617 applies, and for Digest with AKA, Section 5 of RFC 3310.

Delegating the final check to the SIP server requires sending H(A1) to it. The client and server must therefore trust each other, for example by sharing an administrative domain, and the transport between them MUST be secured (RFC 3588 specifies TLS and IPsec). Because of these risks, the RFC RECOMMENDS the mode where the Diameter server performs the final check.
sections.plainLanguage: Handing the answer key to a guard is risky. Do it only if you trust the guard and the road between the office and the guard is safe. Otherwise keep the key at the office.

messages.note: Nonce and challenge for the SIP 401.

items.label: UAR / UAA
items.desc: User-Authorization: may the user register, and which SIP server serves them.

items.label: SAR / SAA
items.desc: Server-Assignment: record the serving SIP server and download the user profile.

items.label: LIR / LIA
items.desc: Location-Info: find the SIP server for a request's recipient.

items.label: RTR / RTA
items.desc: Registration-Termination: the server ends a registration.

items.label: PPR / PPA
items.desc: Push-Profile: the server sends an updated user profile.

viz.caption: WHERE THE FINAL DIGEST CHECK HAPPENS

left.title: Checked in the Diameter server
left.desc: No Digest-HA1 in the MAA. The credentials go in the MAR. This is the RECOMMENDED mode.

right.title: Delegated to the SIP server
right.desc: A pre-calculated Digest-HA1 is sent in the MAA, saving a round trip. Needs trust and a secured transport.
